responsibility.value: Registers the global exception handling middleware via UseExceptionHandler that catches all unhandled exceptions, maps them to structured JSON error responses (ErrorResponse with Status, Code, Message), and logs every exception through ILogger — defining the single API error shape for every endpoint.

Owns: Registering the ASP.NET Core exception handler pipeline via UseExceptionHandler(errorApp => ...)
Inspecting the caught exception via IExceptionHandlerFeature and pattern-matching it to determine status code, error code, and user-facing message
Mapping AppException → its custom StatusCode + ErrorCode + Message
Mapping all other exceptions → 500 + error.internal + Messages.InternalError
Logging every caught exception at Error level via ILogger
Writing the ErrorResponse as JSON to the HTTP response body
doesNotOwn: Model validation errors (FluentValidation) — those are handled by FluentValidation.AspNetCore's automatic model validation before the action runs, not by this middleware
Authorization failures — those are handled by ASP.NET Core's authorization middleware earlier in the pipeline and produce their own challenge/forbid responses

Application-layer business logic exceptions thrown intentionally — those use AppException which this middleware maps to the correct HTTP status, but the business logic flows through the application services, not this handler
Request-level logging or audit trails — only exception-level logging is done here

collaborators.detail: Pattern-matched in the exception handler switch expression; its StatusCode, ErrorCode, and Message are used directly in the ErrorResponse
Provides standardized error message strings (BadRequest, InternalError) for non-AppException cases
Retrieved from HttpContext.Features to access the caught exception; the sole entry point into the exception details
Resolved from request services; LogError is called for every caught exception with the full exception details

contracts: Every unhandled exception produces a JSON response with Content-Type: application/json and a consistent ErrorResponse shape (Status, Code, Message)

AppException subclasses (NotFoundException, AuthenticationException, AuthorizationException, BusinessException, ConflictException) each contribute their own HTTP status code and error code via the AppException base class properties
ArgumentException (and subclasses) produce HTTP 400 with a generic bad-request error code
All other unexpected exceptions produce HTTP 500 and do not leak internal details — the message is always Messages.InternalError regardless of the actual exception message
assumptions: AppException subclasses are properly initialized with meaningful StatusCode, ErrorCode, and Message values — if a subclass defaults these to 0/empty, the error response will have status 0 and an empty message

The middleware is registered early enough in the pipeline (app.UseErrorHandling() called before UseAuthentication, UseAuthorization, UseMiddleware, MapControllers) to catch exceptions from all downstream middleware and controllers
IExceptionHandlerFeature is always available inside the UseExceptionHandler branch — ASP.NET Core guarantees this when the error branch runs
The JSON serialization defaults (JsonSerializerDefaults.Web) produce camelCase property names matching the ErrorResponse record definition
invariants: No unhandled exception ever reaches the client as a raw ASP.NET Core error page or stack trace — every exception is caught and formatted as JSON
The HTTP response status code is always set explicitly from the AppException or the default mapping — never left at the default 200/500
Internal server errors always use Messages.InternalError as the user-facing message — implementation details are never leaked to the client
failureModes: If the ILogger resolution fails or throws (e.g., misconfigured logging provider), the exception is swallowed by the try/catch-free errorApp.Run — the error response is still written, but logging is lost
If the response cannot be written (client disconnected), WriteAsync throws — this exception is not caught and surfaces to ASP.NET Core's own error handling, which may produce a secondary error
If an AppException subclass has StatusCode == 0 (uninitialized), the response will have HTTP status 0 which most HTTP clients treat as a protocol error
An exception thrown during middleware registration or before this middleware runs (e.g., in UseApplicationLogging or ValidateRequiredSettings) is NOT caught — those are startup exceptions
architecturalNotes: HIGH BLAST RADIUS — every API response that results in an error flows through this middleware. The ErrorResponse shape (Status, Code, Message) is the de facto API error contract; any change here affects all API consumers.

The switch expression maps *all* unhandled exceptions, including framework-level ones (TaskCanceledException, ObjectDisposedException, etc.) to a generic 500 — this is correct behavior but can make debugging transient infrastructure issues harder since the specific exception type is only visible in the log, not the response.

There is no ProblemDetails compliance (RFC 7807) — the ErrorResponse is a custom shape (Status, Code, Message) rather than the standard ProblemDetails type. This is a deliberate simplification but means OpenAPI tooling that expects ProblemDetails won't find it.
The ErrorResponse is a private record inside the MiddlewareExtensions class — it cannot be reused by other parts of the application that might want to produce the same error shape.

The error code strings ('error.bad_request', 'error.internal') follow a dot-notation pattern but no centralized registry of error codes exists — consumers must reverse-engineer which codes can appear.
